blocks.text: The battles of the cranes with the Pygmies near the southern Ocean and the sources of the Nile, about which many writers since Homer have spun many tales, we gladly pass over. Yet the Philosopher asserts that in that fable at least this much is true, that very small men live in those places, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Μεταβάλλουσιν, he says, αἱ γέρανοι ἐκ τῶν Σκυθικῶν εἰς τὰ ἕλη τὰ ἄνω τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ὅθεν ὁ Νεῖλος ῥεῖ. Ἔστι δὲ ὁ τόπος οὗτος, περὶ ὃν οἱ Πυγμαῖοι κατοικοῦσιν. Οὐ γάρ ἐστι τοῦτο μῦθος, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστι κατὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν γένος μικρὸν μὲν, ὥσπερ λέγεται, καὶ αὐτοὶ, καὶ οἱ ἵπποι. Τρωγλοδύται δ᾽ εἰσὶ τὸν βίον. [Metaballousin hai geranoi ek tōn Skythikōn eis ta helē ta anō tēs Aigyptou, hothen ho Neilos rhei. Esti de ho topos houtos, peri hon hoi Pygmaioi katoikousin. Ou gar esti touto mythos, all᾽ esti kata tēn alētheian genos mikron men, hōsper legetai, kai autoi, kai hoi hippoi. Trōglodytai d᾽ eisi ton bion.] From the Scythian regions the cranes migrate to the marshes that lie above Egypt, whence the Nile flows. Around this place the Pygmies live. For this is no fable; in truth, as they say, there is a small race there, both of men and of horses. They lead a Troglodyte life, that is, they live in caves under the earth. Everyone knows that the true sources of the Nile were entirely unknown to the ancients. Here, therefore, by the name Nile is meant the Astaboras, which [col. 77] the ancients believed to be a branch of the Nile, as we have shown elsewhere. The Astaboras rises in places nearest to the Avalites gulf and the trading-post of Mosylon. That is why Aethicus places the sources of the Nile there: And the river Nile, he says, which seems to emerge from the shore of the beginning of the Red Sea, in the place called the Mossylon trading-post. And indeed Nonnosus, sailing about these places on his way from the Homerites to the Axumites, Ἐνέτυχέ τισι μορφὴν μὲν καὶ ἰδέαν ἔχουσιν ἀνθρωπίνην, βραχυτάτοις δὲ τὸ μέγεθος, καὶ μέλασι τὴν χρόαν· ὑπὸ δὲ τριχῶν δεδασυμμένοις διὰ παντὸς τοῦ σώματος· εἵποντο δὲ τοῖς ἀνδράσι καὶ γυναῖκες παραπλήσιαι, καὶ παιδάρια ἔτι βραχύτερα. [Enetyche tisi morphēn men kai idean echousin anthrōpinēn, brachytatois de to megethos, kai melasi tēn chroan; hypo de trichōn dedasymmenois dia pantos tou sōmatos; heiponto de tois andrasi kai gynaikes paraplēsiai, kai paidaria eti brachytera.] came upon certain people, human indeed in form and shape, but very short in stature, black in colour, and hairy over the whole body. The men were followed by women of nearly the same size, and by children still shorter. So Photius in the Excerpts from the history of Nonnosus, who lived under Justinian. Moreover, in Hesychius Νῶβαι [Nōbai] are Πυγμαῖοι [Pygmaioi]: the Nobae, that is, the Nubae, who live in those places. And Strabo, book 17, on the Ethiopians below Egypt: τά τε βοσκήματα αὐτοῖς ἐστι μικρὰ πρόβατα, καὶ αἶγες, καὶ βόες, καὶ κύνες μικροί· τραχεῖς δὲ καὶ μάχιμοι οἰκοῦντες μικροὶ ὄντες. Τάχα δὲ τοὺς Πυγμαίους ἀπὸ τῆς τούτων μικροφυΐας ἐπενόησαν καὶ ἀνέπλασαν· ἑωρακὼς [II, 627] μὲν γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἐξηγεῖται τῶν πίστεως ἀξίων ἀνδρῶν. [ta te boskēmata autois esti mikra probata, kai aiges, kai boes, kai kynes mikroi; tracheis de kai machimoi oikountes mikroi ontes. Tacha de tous Pygmaious apo tēs toutōn mikrophyias epenoēsan kai aneplasan; heōrakōs men gar oudeis exēgeitai tōn pisteōs axiōn andrōn.] Their livestock are small sheep and goats, oxen too, and small dogs. The inhabitants themselves are also tiny, yet rough and warlike. And perhaps on account of their natural smallness (the ancients of those parts) invented the Pygmies. For no one worthy of credit has seen them. That is, Pygmies such as they are imagined to be, three spans tall, such as not even Homer had described. But this invention has as its authors the most fabulous of writers, Megasthenes and Daimachus, of whom Strabo says in book 2: Ἐνεκαίνισαν δὲ καὶ τὴν Ὁμηρικὴν τῶν Πυγμαίων γερανομαχίαν τρισπιθάμους εἴποντες· [Enekainisan de kai tēn Homērikēn tōn Pygmaiōn geranomachian trispithamous eipontes;] They embellished the Homeric battle of the Pygmies with the cranes, saying that they were three spans tall. The Arabs too report the same on the word of a certain little Greek, who is said to have told it thus to Jacob, son of Isaac, of Siraf: ركبت في بحر الزنج والقتني الريح الي بعض الجزاير فوصلت منها الي مدينة اهلها ناس قاماتهم قدم نراع واكثرهم عور فاجتمع علي منهم جمع وانتهوا بي الي ملكهم فامر بحبسي فحبست في شبه قفص ثم رايتهم في بعض الايام يستعدون القتال وقالوا لنا عدو ياتينا في هذا الاوان فلم يلبث الي ان طلعت عليهم عصابة من الغرانيق وكان عورهم من نقرها اعينهم فاخذت عصي وشددت عليها وهربت واكرموني لذلك [rakibtu fī baḥr al-Zanj wa-alqatnī al-rīḥ ilā baʿḍ al-jazāyir fa-waṣaltu minhā ilā madīna ahluhā nās qāmātuhum qadm nrāʿ wa-aktharuhum ʿūr fa-ijtamaʿa ʿalayya minhum jamʿ wa-intahaw bī ilā malikihim fa-amara bi-ḥabsī fa-ḥubistu fī shibh qafaṣ thumma raʾaytuhum fī baʿḍ al-ayyām yastaʿiddūn al-qitāl wa-qālū lanā ʿaduww yaʾtīnā fī hādhā al-awān fa-lam yalbath ilā an ṭalaʿat ʿalayhim ʿiṣāba min al-gharānīq wa-kāna ʿawaruhum min naqrihā aʿyunahum fa-akhadhtu ʿaṣā wa-shadadtu ʿalayhā wa-harabat wa-akramūnī li-dhālik] I was once sailing on the Zanj sea, and the wind drove me to a certain island. When I reached its town, I found the inhabitants to be a cubit tall, and most of them one-eyed. A crowd of them gathered around me and led me to [col. 78] their king. He ordered that I be held captive, and I was thrown into a kind of cage. When one day I saw them preparing for war, they said that an enemy was threatening and would soon fall upon them. Not long after, an army of cranes rose up against them. And they were one-eyed because the cranes had pecked out their eyes. But I took a stick and charged at them, and they flew off and fled. For this deed I was held in honour among them.
